title.en: Unit 3 Notes — Drawings for Residential Building Planning
title.gu: Unit 3 Notes — Drawings for Residential Building Planning

h.en: 3.1 The data drawing — what a complete set contains
h.gu: 3.1 The data drawing — what a complete set contains

items.syllabus_item: 3.1.1 Data drawing: detailed plan, elevation, section, site plan, schedule of openings, construction notes with specifications, area statement

body.en:
Data drawing means the complete information set from which a building can be sanctioned, estimated and built without visiting the designer. The syllabus names its parts — learn each part's job, because examination questions ask 'what does a working set contain' and site life punishes any missing part.

Detailed plan. The horizontal section taken just above sill level (above window sills, below lintels), drawn to 1:50: wall thicknesses (external 230 mm, internal 115–150 mm typical), every room dimensioned in chains (room sizes, wall-to-wall, overall), door/window positions with schedule symbols D/W/V, floor levels, steps, sanitary fittings positions, staircase with UP/DN arrows, north point. The plan is the master — elevation, section and foundation plan inherit its geometry.

Elevation. The front (and side where needed) vertical view: ground and plinth lines, floor-to-floor heights, door-window heights with sill/lintel levels, chajja and parapet, roof form, materials/finishes indicated, overall height for bye-law check. Elevation proves prospect/elegance (2.3) and the sanction height.

Section. A vertical cut (through staircase and bath-WC wherever possible so maximum construction is revealed): foundation depth and steps, plinth/DPC, floor build-ups, lintel/slab levels, stair rise-tread and headroom, ceiling and parapet — every vertical size the elevation cannot give. At least one section; two (longitudinal + cross) for the G+1 set.

Site plan. Small scale (1:200–1:500): plot boundaries and sizes, margins/setbacks left, building footprint, approach road and its width, north point, neighbouring plots/structures, drainage direction, septic/soak or sewer connection, water line, trees retained. Site plan proves bye-law compliance on the plot.

Schedule of openings. A table: symbol (D1, D2, W1, V1), size (width × height in mm), number, sill height, type/material/frame-shutter notes and location hints. The carpenter, fabricator, estimator and checker all work from this one table — a door missing from the schedule is a door missing from the estimate.

Construction notes with specifications. The written half of the drawing: materials and mixes (e.g., '230 brick masonry in CM 1:6', 'RCC M20'), DPC, flooring, joinery timber/section, painting, waterproofing, curing — short numbered notes placed beside the views, converting geometry into quality. Notes must never contradict the dimensions; where they meet, specification governs quality and dimension governs size.

Area statement. The bye-law table: plot area, permissible FSI, proposed built-up per floor, total and FSI achieved, ground coverage, margin table, room-area check where required (Unit 2 arithmetic, presented formally). The sanctioning engineer checks this first — an area statement that does not tally with the plans stops the file.

Set discipline. Same title block, sheet numbering (DWG 01…), scale stated per view, revision noted; plan-elevation-section aligned where the sheet allows; every symbol used appears in the schedule/legend. Draw the set as one document, not five separate pictures.

h.en: 3.1 Load-bearing structure — single-storey 2 BHK with staircase and its foundation plan
h.gu: 3.1 Load-bearing structure — single-storey 2 BHK with staircase and its foundation plan

items.syllabus_item: 3.1.1 Drawing of Single storey Load Bearing residential building (2 BHK) with staircase; 3.1.2 Foundation plan of Load bearing structure

body.en:
The structural idea. In a load-bearing building, walls carry everything: slab → walls → strip footings → soil. There are no columns; therefore wall thickness is structure — external and internal load walls typically 230 mm (one brick) in burnt brick/block masonry, partition (non-load) walls 115 mm. Suitable for single/double storey on firm soil; openings are limited because every hole cuts the load path, and lintels bridge each opening.

Drawing the 2 BHK plan (the sheet's core). Start from the Unit 2 line plan of two bedrooms + living + kitchen + bath-WC; thicken walls; align wet areas; place the staircase (commonly in a corner/external flight for a single storey, or an internal dog-legged flight where a future floor is planned — Card 3.3 designs it). Doors 1000/900 × 2100/2000, windows scheduled W1/W2 with ventilators over bath-WC. Dimension chains: wall lengths, openings positions from corners, overall size; show plinth steps, verandah and chajja line (dotted over windows) where applicable.

Elevation and section. Elevation: plinth 450 mm, floor-to-ceiling 3000 mm, lintel 2100, slab/parapet above; pitched or flat roof as designed. Section AA (through stair and WC): foundation steps (below), floor on filling, DPC at plinth, lintels, slab with bearing on walls (minimum bearing lengths matter — slab/wall junction drawn honestly), stair waist with headroom ≥ 2000 mm, parapet 600–900 mm with coping.

Foundation plan (3.1.2) — how to draw it. It is a plan of only the footings, looking down with walls removed mentally: (1) draw wall centre lines chain-thin; (2) draw footing edges (width lines) solid where visible at excavation level, or as prescribed — convention in student sheets: footing outlines with dashed hidden portions under plinth; (3) show steps widths at junctions, foundation for the staircase wall and verandah columns/piers if any; (4) dimension footing widths and offsets from centre lines, and state foundation depth (e.g., 900–1200 mm below GL to firm strata, per soil). Junctions (L, T, X) need care: footing widths merge; the wider wall's footing governs.

Foundation section logic. Under a 230 wall carrying one storey: PCC bed (1:4:8 or 1:5:10, 75–100 thick, projecting 100–150 each side) → stepped brick/stone footing in 2–3 steps (each step offset ≈ 50 mm per side per course height) widening to the required footing width (Numerical 3.3) → masonry up to plinth → 40–50 mm DPC → wall above. Depth protects against seasonal soil movement and reaches bearing strata; width keeps soil pressure ≤ safe bearing capacity (SBC).

Load-bearing drawing traps. Staircase drawn without its foundation wall/pier; openings shown in plan but lintel missing in section; wall thickness changed between plan and foundation plan; floor levels differing between elevation and section. Cross-check the three views dimension by dimension — the set is one building.

h.en: 3.2 Framed structure — two-storey (G+1) 2 BHK, foundation plan and the column grid
h.gu: 3.2 Framed structure — two-storey (G+1) 2 BHK, foundation plan and the column grid

items.syllabus_item: 3.2.1 Drawing of Two storey Framed Structure (G+1) residential building (2 BHK) with staircase (data drawing); 3.2.2 Foundation plan of Framed Structure

body.en:
The structural idea. In a framed building an RCC skeleton — footings → columns → beams → slabs — carries all loads; walls become partitions (115–230 mm filler) placed anywhere between columns. Consequences for drawing: the column grid decides the plan; floors can repeat or vary; large openings and cantilevers become possible; the set grows extra sheets (column layout, beam/slab layouts in structural sets).

Planning the G+1 set. Fix a regular grid (spans 3–4.5 m economical) from the ground-floor line plan: living + kitchen + bed + bath-WC below; two bedrooms + bath above the same wet stack; staircase dog-legged in one grid bay, serving both floors with a common entrance lobby. Ground and first floor plans are drawn separately (openings/stair well differ), one typical section through stair, front elevation showing both storeys, balcony and parapet; roof/terrace plan in fuller sets.

Foundation plan of a framed structure (3.2.2). Draw: (1) grid lines (chain) with bubbles A, B, C / 1, 2, 3; (2) column positions as filled/outlined squares (230 × 230 to 230 × 400 typical residential, per structural design); (3) footing outlines (isolated square/rectangular pads, eccentric at plot-boundary columns) dimensioned and scheduled F1, F2 with sizes and depths in a footing table; (4) plinth/tie beams connecting footings (also on the same or a companion layout); (5) staircase and lift (if any) foundations. Dimension grid spacings cumulatively so site setting-out starts from two reference lines.

Isolated footing — what the section must show. Column from above with starter bars; footing as reinforced pad (uniform) or sloped/stepped pad; PCC lean bed 75–100 below; depth to firm strata (min ≈ 1.2–1.5 m typical for G+1 on average soil — design value rules); backfill and plinth beam at top tying columns against differential settlement and carrying ground-floor walls. Boundary columns get combined/eccentric footings so the footing never crosses the plot line.

Framed vs load-bearing on paper. Load-bearing foundation plan = continuous strips under walls; framed = discrete pads on a grid. In plans, framed walls align to grid faces with column squares projecting honestly (never hide a column inside a wall line that is drawn thinner than the column). Beam positions under slab are hidden lines on floor plans where they affect ceilings/openings.

Set list for 3.2.1. Site plan, ground + first floor plans, elevation, sections, foundation plan, schedule of openings, notes/specifications, area statement (FSI now consumed over two floors — Numerical 2.1's arithmetic on this unit's sheet), plus RCC detail sheet (Card 3.4).

h.en: 3.3 Staircase — planning and design (rise and tread)
h.gu: 3.3 Staircase — planning and design (rise and tread)

items.syllabus_item: 3.1.1/3.2.1 Planning and design of staircase: Rise and Tread for residential and public building

body.en:
Stair vocabulary first. Rise (riser): vertical height of one step. Tread (going of a step): horizontal depth you stand on. Going: total horizontal run of a flight. Flight: unbroken series of steps (3 minimum, ≈12–15 maximum). Landing: flat platform between flights (depth ≥ stair width). Nosing: tread edge projecting slightly over the riser. Waist: thickness of the sloped slab under steps. Headroom: clear vertical height above the tread nosing line (≥ 2000 mm, prefer 2100+). Handrail/balustrade: ≈ 900 mm above nosings (900–1000).

Comfort rules (learn as a set). Residential: rise 150–180 mm (design 150–160), tread 250–300 mm (design 270–300); public buildings: rise 130–160, tread 280–320 (more feet, more flow). Comfort formula:

2 × Rise + Tread = 550 to 700 mm (aim ≈ 600-630 mm)Rise × Tread ≈ 40000 to 45000 mm² (checking companion rule)

All rises in a flight equal (a changed last riser trips the whole building's memory); width residential ≥ 900–1000 mm (public 1200–2000 by crowd), landing ≥ width; stair located for direct entry, fire escape logic, and lighted/ventilated (a window on the stair wall at landing level is planning, not luck).

Types by plan form. Straight flight; L (quarter-turn) with landing or winders; dog-legged (two parallel flights, half landing — the residential standard in this subject); open-well (flights around a central gap, allows a lift); U/three-quarter, bifurcated and spiral for special cases. Winders (tapered treads at turns) are avoided in exam designs — landings are safer.

Design procedure (practised in Numerical 3.1). 1) Risers = floor height ÷ chosen rise, rounded up to a whole number; recompute exact rise. 2) Treads in a flight = risers in that flight − 1 (the landing/floor is the last 'tread'). 3) Choose flight split about the landing; going = treads × tread; check stair-room length = goings + landing. 4) Verify comfort formula, headroom over the flight below (section through stair), width and landing depth; then draw plan (arrow UP from entry floor, DN from above, tread lines numbered) and section (step profile over waist slab).

Drawing the stair. Plan: show from the floor it serves — steps visible below the cutting plane solid, steps above the cut broken by a diagonal break line with UP/DN arrows; number of risers written ('12 R 150'). Section: step teeth over the waist slab (waist ≈ 120–150 residential), railing line parallel to nosings at 900, headroom dimension vertical from nosing line to soffit above. Staircase foundation/wall or supporting beam appears in foundation plan and section.

h.en: 3.4 RCC details — footing, column, beam, lintel, chajja, staircase and slab
h.gu: 3.4 RCC details — footing, column, beam, lintel, chajja, staircase and slab

items.syllabus_item: 3.2.3 Details of RCC footing, Column, Beam, Chajjas, Lintel, Staircase and slab

body.en:
Why a separate RCC detail sheet. Plans say where members are; RCC details say how they are reinforced: bar diameters, spacing, bends, laps, cover — the information the bar-bender and checker work from. The diploma reader must read size + steel together; final quantities come from the structural design, but standard residential forms recur.

Footing (isolated). Section + plan of bars: bottom mesh both ways (main and distribution become a grid in a pad), bars bent up at ends where designed, column starter (dowel) bars L-bent into the footing, clear cover 50 mm against soil (with PCC bed), development length into the column. Drawing shows footing size/depth, bar marks (e.g., '10 ∅ @ 150 c/c both ways') and the column centred or eccentric as designed.

Column. Section: longitudinal bars at corners (and sides for rectangular), lateral ties/links at closer spacing near ends (confinement), lap positions staggered away from joints; plan position tied to the grid (Card 3.2). Sizes change with height in tall frames — the drawing schedules C1, C2 by floor.

Beam. Longitudinal section + cross-section: main tension steel at bottom (mid-span), top steel at supports (over columns where continuous), stirrups — vertical links closer near supports (shear is highest there), side-face bars in deep beams; cover 25 mm; bar curtailment/bent-up bars shown by the structural drawing. Read: bottom bars sag-zone, top bars hog-zone — steel follows tension.

Lintel. A small beam over every opening: bearing ≥ 150–200 mm each side (or to wall end), depth ≈ 100–150 for residential spans with nominal 2 bars bottom + stirrups/hangers as drawn; where walls continue above, lintel band at that level ties the masonry. Chajja: the sloped/level sunshade slab cantilevered over openings (450–600 projection), thin at tip (≈50–75) thicker at wall, main steel on top (cantilever tension is at top — the classic site error is bottom steel in a chajja) anchored into the lintel/wall.

Slab. Plan + sections: one-way slab (main bars in short direction, distribution in long, bars bent up/cranked at supports) vs two-way (both ways main with corner torsional care); top steel over supports, extra bars around openings/stair well trimmers; cover 15–20 mm; thickness ≈ 100–125 residential spans. Stair well opening in slab is framed by trimmer beams — shown on slab layout, not discovered on site.

Staircase (RCC). Waist-slab type (common): main bars run up the slope at bottom, distribution across, top bars at landing junctions, each step cast monolithic; landing slab steel both ways; railing posts fixed to waist/stringer. The section (Card 3.3) plus a bar note is the site instruction.

Reading rules for every RCC detail. Member size, concrete grade (M20 typical), bar mark = diameter + spacing/type, cover, lap/anchorage, and a schedule matching symbols between plan and section. Missing cover or spacing is a missing drawing, whatever the picture quality.

title.en: Numerical 3.1 — Design a dog-legged staircase for a residence
title.gu: Numerical 3.1 — Design a dog-legged staircase for a residence

body.en:
Given. Floor-to-floor height = 3200 mm. Residential stair: try rise 160 mm, tread 250 mm, stair width 1000 mm, half landing. The line plan has allotted a stair hall 4300 mm long - to be checked.

Find. Risers, treads, exact rise, going, total stair length, and whether the allotted hall works.

Step 1. Find the number of risers (round up to a whole number).

risers = 3200 / 160 = 20.0 → adopt 20 risers

Step 2. Recompute the exact rise so every riser stays equal.

exact rise = 3200 / 20 = 160 mm

Step 3. Split the risers equally about the half landing and find the treads (treads = risers − 1 in each flight).

flight 1: 10 risers → 9 treads ; flight 2: 10 risers → 9 treads

Step 4. Find the going of one flight and the total stair-hall length.

going = 9 × 250 = 2250 mm ; hall = 2250 + landing 1000 + 2250 = 5500 mm

Step 5. Check the comfort rule.

2R + T = 2(160) + 250 = 570 mm (within 550-700 ✓) ; R × T = 160 × 250 = 40000 mm² ✓

Step 6. Compare with the allotted hall: 5500 mm needed but only 4300 mm given. Correct decision: enlarge/re-plan the stair hall to 5500 mm at the line-plan stage - do NOT squeeze treads below comfort or make risers unequal.

Final answer.

╔ 20 risers of 160 mm; tread 250 mm; two flights of 9 treads; landing 1000 mm; provide stair hall 5500 mm long ╗

Validity check. Stair arithmetic belongs to the planning stage (Unit 2): the plan grows around the stair, never the reverse. Headroom (≥ 2000 mm above every nosing) must still be verified in the section.
body.gu:
Given. Floor-to-floor height = 3200 mm. Residential stair: try rise 160 mm, tread 250 mm, stair width 1000 mm, half landing. The line plan has allotted a stair hall 4300 mm long - to be checked.

Find. Risers, treads, exact rise, going, total stair length, and whether the allotted hall works.

Step 1. Find the number of risers (round up to a whole number).

risers = 3200 / 160 = 20.0 → adopt 20 risers

Step 2. Recompute the exact rise so every riser stays equal.

exact rise = 3200 / 20 = 160 mm

Step 3. Split the risers equally about the half landing and find the treads (treads = risers − 1 in each flight).

flight 1: 10 risers → 9 treads ; flight 2: 10 risers → 9 treads

Step 4. Find the going of one flight and the total stair-hall length.

going = 9 × 250 = 2250 mm ; hall = 2250 + landing 1000 + 2250 = 5500 mm

Step 5. Check the comfort rule.

2R + T = 2(160) + 250 = 570 mm (within 550-700 ✓) ; R × T = 160 × 250 = 40000 mm² ✓

Step 6. Compare with the allotted hall: 5500 mm needed but only 4300 mm given. Correct decision: enlarge/re-plan the stair hall to 5500 mm at the line-plan stage - do NOT squeeze treads below comfort or make risers unequal.

Final answer.

╔ 20 risers of 160 mm; tread 250 mm; two flights of 9 treads; landing 1000 mm; provide stair hall 5500 mm long ╗

Validity check. Stair arithmetic belongs to the planning stage (Unit 2): the plan grows around the stair, never the reverse. Headroom (≥ 2000 mm above every nosing) must still be verified in the section.

title.en: Numerical 3.2 — Width of a load-bearing strip footing from SBC
title.gu: Numerical 3.2 — Width of a load-bearing strip footing from SBC

body.en:
Given. A 230 mm wall of a single-storey house carries a service load of 72 kN per metre run (given from load estimation). Safe bearing capacity (SBC) of soil = 100 kN/m². Ignore footing self-weight for this exercise (state the assumption).

Find. Required footing width; choose a practical width and the PCC bed width.

Step 1. Find the width so soil pressure equals SBC (1 metre run).

required width B = load per metre / SBC = 72 / 100 = 0.72 m

Step 2. Round up to a practical masonry module.

adopt footing (bottom step) width = 750 mm

Step 3. Give the PCC bed its projection beyond the bottom step (100 mm each side).

PCC bed width = 750 + 2 × 100 = 950 mm ; check pressure = 72 / 0.75 = 96 kN/m² ≤ 100 ✓

Final answer.

╔ Footing width 750 mm on a 950 mm wide PCC bed; soil pressure 96 kN/m² within SBC ╗

Validity check. Stepped masonry (Card 3.1 section) climbs from 750 mm at the bottom step to the 230 mm wall in 2–3 steps of ≈ 50 mm offset per side; foundation depth still needs firm strata (commonly 900–1200 mm) — width and depth answer different questions.

title.en: Numerical 3.3 — Area statement for the G+1 framed set (FSI tally)
title.gu: Numerical 3.3 — Area statement for the G+1 framed set (FSI tally)

body.en:
Given. Plot 15.0 m × 20.0 m. Ground floor built-up 132 m²; first floor built-up 126 m²; permissible FSI 1.5; permissible ground coverage 60%. (Exercise bye-law values.)

Find. FSI consumed, permissible built-up, coverage check, and the balance FSI.

Step 1. Find plot area and permissible total built-up.

plot = 15.0 × 20.0 = 300 m² ; permissible = 1.5 × 300 = 450 m²

Step 2. Add the proposal and find FSI consumed.

proposed = 132 + 126 = 258 m² ; FSI used = 258 / 300 = 0.86

Step 3. Check ground coverage.

coverage = 132 / 300 × 100 = 44 % ≤ 60 % ✓

Step 4. Find the unused FSI area.

balance = 450 − 258 = 192 m²

Final answer.

╔ FSI used 0.86 of 1.5 allowed; coverage 44% passes; 192 m² built-up may still be added within rules ╗

Validity check. This table, signed, is the area statement of Card 3.1 — numbers must be traceable to the two floor plans (measure their built-up outlines), not invented at the table.

q.en: What is a data (working) drawing set? Name its parts.
q.gu: What is a data (working) drawing set? Name its parts.

a.en: The complete sanction-and-build set: site plan, detailed plans, elevation, sections, foundation plan, schedule of openings, construction notes/specifications and area statement.
a.gu: The complete sanction-and-build set: site plan, detailed plans, elevation, sections, foundation plan, schedule of openings, construction notes/specifications and area statement.

q.en: In a load-bearing building, what carries the slab load to the soil?
q.gu: In a load-bearing building, what carries the slab load to the soil?

a.en: The walls themselves, through continuous strip footings under them - hence wall thickness is structural (typically 230 mm).
a.gu: The walls themselves, through continuous strip footings under them - hence wall thickness is structural (typically 230 mm).

q.en: What extra plan does a framed building's foundation need compared with load-bearing?
q.gu: What extra plan does a framed building's foundation need compared with load-bearing?

a.en: A column-grid foundation plan: grid bubbles, column squares, isolated footing sizes (F1, F2...) and plinth/tie beams - pads on a grid instead of strips under walls.
a.gu: A column-grid foundation plan: grid bubbles, column squares, isolated footing sizes (F1, F2...) and plinth/tie beams - pads on a grid instead of strips under walls.

q.en: State the comfort rule for stairs and test R=160, T=270.
q.gu: State the comfort rule for stairs and test R=160, T=270.

a.en: 2R + T should be 550-700 mm. 2×160+270 = 590 mm - comfortable. (R×T = 43200 also in range.)
a.gu: 2R + T should be 550-700 mm. 2×160+270 = 590 mm - comfortable. (R×T = 43200 also in range.)

q.en: Floor height 3000 mm, rise chosen 150 mm. How many risers and treads in one straight flight?
q.gu: Floor height 3000 mm, rise chosen 150 mm. How many risers and treads in one straight flight?

a.en: Risers = 3000/150 = 20. Treads = risers − 1 = 19 (the upper floor is the last tread).
a.gu: Risers = 3000/150 = 20. Treads = risers − 1 = 19 (the upper floor is the last tread).

q.en: What does the schedule of openings contain?
q.gu: What does the schedule of openings contain?

a.en: Symbol, size (width × height), number, sill height and type/material notes for every door, window and ventilator (D1, W1, V...).
a.gu: Symbol, size (width × height), number, sill height and type/material notes for every door, window and ventilator (D1, W1, V...).

q.en: In an RCC chajja, where is the main steel and why?
q.gu: In an RCC chajja, where is the main steel and why?

a.en: At the TOP - a chajja is a cantilever, so tension is at the top near the wall; bottom steel there is the classic site error.
a.gu: At the TOP - a chajja is a cantilever, so tension is at the top near the wall; bottom steel there is the classic site error.

q.en: What is headroom in a staircase and its minimum?
q.gu: What is headroom in a staircase and its minimum?

a.en: Clear vertical height above the tread nosing line to the soffit above; at least 2000 mm (preferably 2100 mm), checked in the section through the stair.
a.gu: Clear vertical height above the tread nosing line to the soffit above; at least 2000 mm (preferably 2100 mm), checked in the section through the stair.

q.en: Why is the section taken through the staircase and WC?
q.gu: Why is the section taken through the staircase and WC?

a.en: That cut reveals the most construction at once: foundation, stair rise-tread and headroom, WC floor/loft levels, slab and parapet heights.
a.gu: That cut reveals the most construction at once: foundation, stair rise-tread and headroom, WC floor/loft levels, slab and parapet heights.

q.en: Cover in RCC: give the values for footing and slab.
q.gu: Cover in RCC: give the values for footing and slab.

a.en: Footing ≈ 50 mm (against soil/PCC bed); slab ≈ 15-20 mm (beam/column ≈ 25-40 mm as per structural drawing).
a.gu: Footing ≈ 50 mm (against soil/PCC bed); slab ≈ 15-20 mm (beam/column ≈ 25-40 mm as per structural drawing).

q.en: What is the difference between footing width and foundation depth decisions?
q.gu: What is the difference between footing width and foundation depth decisions?

a.en: Width keeps soil pressure within SBC (load ÷ SBC). Depth reaches firm, season-safe strata. Both appear in the foundation section.
a.gu: Width keeps soil pressure within SBC (load ÷ SBC). Depth reaches firm, season-safe strata. Both appear in the foundation section.
